subject: Wavelength: Post-demo model slate, benchmarks & next steps
messages:
From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo@redwood.inference>

Cc: 
Date: Fri, 4 Jun 2027 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Wavelength demo — recommended model slate and quick recap

Hi Theo / team,

Thanks again for the time today — great discussion and helpful context on the 2 workloads you emphasized (short-form summarization for support triage, and high-throughput chat completions for the customer-facing assistant). Per our demo, I pulled together a concise recommended slate with the tradeoffs we saw during the session and a few artifacts attached: rwd_model_slate_v1.pdf (one-pager), benchmarks_wavelength_20270607.csv, and a prompt pack we used (prompt_sets_wavelength.zip).

High-level recommended slate (baseline -> high-quality -> fallback):
1) Redwood-Realtime-7B-INT8 (baseline) — why: consistent sub-150ms median token latency at 512-context on our Dedicated 1 pool; cost-efficient with INT8 paths and KV prefix caching. Expected on your workloads: good extractive summarization F1 (~0.78) and solid conversational coherence. Estimated hosted cost (1M tokens): ~$140.

2) Open-Opt-30B-16k (quality) — why: strongest quality on multi-turn reasoning / long-context summarization in our evals; higher latency (~420ms median token at 1k context) and higher cost due to model size and memory footprint. Expected quality lift: +6–9% precision/recall on your internal support labels. Estimated hosted cost (1M tokens): ~$620.

3) Redwood-Fallback-3B (fallback / fall-through) — why: very cheap, sub-100ms latency for simple rewrites and safety filtering; use as post-filter or cold fallback when high-tier capacity is full. Estimated hosted cost (1M tokens): ~$40.

Notes and tradeoffs (short):
- Latency numbers assume our default batching and KV cache enabled; cold-start or long-context leads to higher p95. See latency_cost_breakdown.xlsx for sensitivity.
- Quality numbers are vs. your sample support dataset we ran during the demo; I included the raw CSV of per-prompt scores and the prompt sets we used.
- Regression risk: when swapping to INT8 we recommend a small eval set (50–100 critical prompts) as a regression guardrail before rolling to production.

Proposed next steps:
- Confirm which workload you want to optimize first (support summarization vs. assistant).
- Quick follow-up to walk procurement through Dedicated vs. Hosted pricing and the committed throughput options (I can pull commercial numbers).
- Run a short pilot: 2-week sandbox with your 1k sample prompts (we can set up a locked eval with the three candidate engines).

Available times next week to sync on pricing/procurement: Tue 6/8 10–11am PT or Wed 6/9 2–3pm PT.

Thanks — attaching the artifacts referenced above.

Best,
Mateo Alvarez
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
Mateo@redwood.inference

Thanks Mateo — this is helpful. A few quick clarifications before we loop procurement:

- Can you confirm how the benchmark CSV maps to our labels? I need to see per-label precision/recall for the summarization set (we care a lot about recall on symptom extraction).
- For the Realtime-7B-INT8 baseline: what p95 latency should we expect under a 200 RPS sustained load? Also curious how batching changes when we enable strict latency SLOs.
- For the Open-Opt-30B: curious if there are quantized variants you recommend (we're sensitive to cost but may accept slower responses for higher accuracy).

One more ask: please include the prompt sets and a short doc describing the regression guardrail you recommend so our ML engineers can review.

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.inference>
To: Mateo Alvarez <mateo@redwood.inference>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.inference>
Date: Mon, 7 Jun 2027 11:22:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: Wavelength demo — mapping benchmarks + quantization notes (internal)

Mateo / Marissa — internal notes and clarifications to drop into the scheduled call:

1) Benchmarks mapping: the CSV (benchmarks_wavelength_20270607.csv) contains per-prompt scores and the columns are: prompt_id, label_type, reference, model, precision, recall, f1, latency_ms_median, latency_ms_p95, tokens_generated. We ran on your provided support sample (n=1,200) with simulated 200 RPS using our load harness; see the sheet '200RPS_sim' for aggregated p95 numbers. For symptom-extraction (label_type = 'symptom') recall differences: Realtime-7B-INT8 = 0.72, Open-Opt-30B-16k = 0.80, Redwood-Fallback-3B = 0.60.

2) Latency under sustained 200 RPS:
- Redwood-Realtime-7B-INT8: median token latency ~140ms, p95 token latency ~420ms under our Dedicated 1 baseline with autoscaling enabled.
- Open-Opt-30B-16k: median token latency ~360ms, p95 ~920ms (note: large variance with long-context requests).
- Redwood-Fallback-3B: median ~90ms, p95 ~210ms.

3) Batching & latency SLOs: enabling strict <250ms p95 requires reducing batching window and setting smaller target batch sizes which increases per-token cost ~12–18% on average; we should present both base and low-latency cost numbers.

4) Quantized variants: for Open-Opt-30B we have a 4-bit quantized path (Open-Opt-30B-4q) that reduces memory and cost by ~28% with a small quality delta (F1 drop ~0.02 on avg). Recommend offering that as a middle ground. It's included in the attachment row 'Open-Opt-30B-4q' in the CSV.

5) Regression guardrail doc: see the small checklist in rwd_model_slate_v1.pdf (page 2). Short version: holdout set (50–100 golden prompts), automated diff alerts (F1 drop > 0.03), sample-based human review on any planed quantization/weight changes.

I'll be on the call Tue 6/8 to answer the deeper infra questions; Mateo — please share the HubSpot deal link and any procurement docs you plan to use.

Thanks,
Karthik
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
